name: Suggestibility
statement: Under questioning by someone in authority, people accept suggested details and change answers under pressure, and how much they do varies between individuals.
meaning: Interrogative suggestibility is a narrower idea than the everyday word. Gudjonsson and Clark defined it in 1986 as the extent to which, within a closed social interaction, people come to accept messages communicated during formal questioning, so that their behavioural response is affected. Kassin and his co-authors quote that definition from page 84 of the 1986 paper, and this entry takes it from them rather than from the original, which could not be obtained. Two things are measured at once. The first is yielding to a leading question. The second is changing an answer after being told the answers were wrong, which is a response to interpersonal pressure rather than to the content of the question. Gudjonsson's scales score these separately as Yield and Shift. The forensic claim built on top is that suspects and witnesses who score high are at greater risk of giving statements that are wrong, and in the extreme of confessing to crimes they did not commit. Two populations carry most of the applied weight: criminal suspects under police interrogation, and children questioned about alleged abuse.

origin.note: The 1984 paper introduced the Gudjonsson Suggestibility Scale, the instrument that made the construct measurable. The theoretical model came two years later, in Gudjonsson and Clark's 1986 paper in Social Behaviour, which is where the standard definition is stated. Neither paper was read for this entry. The scale is described here from Kassin and Gudjonsson's 2004 monograph, from the same authors' 2025 update and from Hein and colleagues' 2021 psychometric study, and the definition is quoted as those authors quote it.

evidence: The scale is a memory test with a social trap in it. A narrative paragraph is read aloud, on GSS 1 an account of a woman attacked during a holiday in Spain and robbed of her handbag. The subject recalls it, then answers 20 questions of which 15 are subtly misleading. Yield 1 counts how many of the 15 are accepted, with a maximum of 15. The subject is then told firmly that there were many errors and that every question must be answered again. Yield 2 counts acceptances on the second pass, and Shift counts changed answers in either direction, with a maximum of 20. Yield and Shift are summed for Total Suggestibility, maximum 35. Hein, Scheuble, Beauducel and Leue put a German online GSS 1 to 560 students, mean age 24.20, and recovered the two expected factors. They recruited 593 and excluded 33 for insufficient German. Their internal consistencies were 0.43 for Yield 1, 0.65 for Yield 2 and 0.66 for Shift. Their means sat below the manual's norms: Yield 1 1.44 against Gudjonsson's 4.6, Yield 2 1.99 against 5.6, Shift 1.81 against 2.9 and Total 3.25 against 7.5. Frumkin, Lally and Sexton reported 334 people assessed in United States forensic cases, and their abstract notes that the manual gives samples only from Iceland and Great Britain. They found the pattern Gudjonsson reports: Yield 1 is more affected by intellectual and cognitive variables, while Shift, and to a lesser extent Yield 2, track emotional and personality ones. Kassin and Gudjonsson summarise the correlates as poor memory, high anxiety, low self-esteem and lack of assertiveness, and report that scores rise under prolonged sleep deprivation and alcohol withdrawal. The laboratory work on false confession runs on a different paradigm. Kassin and Kiechel recruited 79 undergraduates and accused them of crashing a computer by hitting a forbidden ALT key. Four were dropped as suspicious, leaving 75. The pace of the typing task was slow at 43 letters a minute or fast at 67, and a confederate either did or did not claim to have seen the key pressed. Of the 75, 69% signed a confession, 28% told a waiting stranger they had done it, and 9% invented details of how. The conditions matter more than the average. With a slow pace and no witness, 34.78% signed and none internalised or confabulated. With a fast pace and a witness, all 17 subjects signed, 65% internalised and 35% confabulated. The four cells differed on all three measures, with chi-square on three degrees of freedom of 23.84 for signing, 37.61 for internalising and 18.0 for confabulating. Redlich and Goodman ran the paradigm across ages 12 to 26. Kassin and Gudjonsson report their rates as 78% among 12- to 13-year-olds, 72% among 15- to 16-year-olds and 59% among 18- to 26-year-olds, with GSS scores predicting who signed. That paper could not be obtained, and those figures stand here as the review reports them. Children's suggestibility is tested differently again. Leichtman and Ceci sent a man called Sam Stone on a visit of about two minutes to 176 preschoolers, then interviewed them once a week for four weeks and again at ten weeks, asking finally about a ripped book and a soiled teddy bear that never happened. No control child made a false allegation in free narrative, and 10% of the youngest control children's answers to direct probes were wrong. Where the interviews had carried the two suggestions, 21% of the 3- to 4-year-olds volunteered a misdeed unprompted, 53% of their probe answers endorsed one, 35% said they had seen it, and 12% held to that after a gentle challenge. Adding a prior stereotype of Sam Stone as clumsy and bumbling pushed the free-narrative figure to 46% and the probe figure to 72%. Overall accuracy fell from 96% in the control group to 83%, 72% and 64% across the three manipulated groups, all ps < .05, with a large age effect, F(1, 146) = 76.55, p < .0001. Videotapes of three of the children were shown at two conferences to 119 researchers and clinicians who work on children's testimony, and the majority of both audiences could not reliably tell which reports were true.

replication.headline: That people sign false confessions in the laboratory repeats reliably, at rates from 8% to 100% depending on the setup, and the pooled link between suggestibility and confessing is large in field samples and small in experiments.
replication.detail: Horselenberg, Merckelbach and Josephs ran the closest thing to a direct replication of the computer-crash study, with 34 female undergraduates and a harsher setup. The forbidden key was SHIFT rather than ALT, the experimenter herself claimed to have seen it pressed, and signing cost 80% of the fee, which the paper gives as $2 instead of $10. Rates went up rather than down. Twenty-seven of 34, or 82%, signed, 14 or 42% took responsibility in conversation with a stranger, and 19 or 58% supplied details of when and how. The individual-difference prediction failed completely. Three MANOVAs against compliance, GSS suggestibility, fantasy proneness, dissociation and cognitive failures returned nothing, all F(1, 25) < 1.5 and p > .2 for signing, all F(1, 29) < 2.1 and p > .15 for internalising and confabulating. The same group then showed how fragile the rate is. In their 2006 study 1, 72 students were accused of hitting the plausible Windows key or the implausible F12 key, and 16 were dropped for seeing through the setup. Of the remaining 56, 77% against 58% signed, a difference that did not reach significance at Fisher's exact p = 0.16. Internalisation appeared only in the Windows condition, in 26% of the confessors there, Fisher's exact p = 0.01. Study 2 told students they would owe about 250 euros for the damage; nine remained after exclusions and one signed, 11%. Study 3 accused students of exam fraud with exclusion from future exams as the penalty; 12 remained after exclusions and one confessed, 8%. Stewart, Woody and Pulos meta-analysed the experimental literature and reached the same conclusion about design. Rates were higher in typing-task studies than in cheating studies, typing speed made no difference, moving the forbidden key somewhere implausible lowered rates, and false-evidence ploys raised them. Otgaar, Schell-Leugers, Howe, De La Fuente Vilar, Houben and Merckelbach pooled the trait evidence in 2021, and their two halves disagree in size. Across four experimental studies, suggestibility separated signers from non-signers by d = 0.33, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.55, while compliance gave d = 0.12, 95% CI -0.18 to 0.43, which does not exclude zero. Across five field studies of prisoners and defendants who said they had confessed falsely, suggestibility gave d = 1.09, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.43, and compliance d = 1.28, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.66, both with heterogeneity above 99%. The single-study record is split the same way. Redlich and Goodman found GSS scores predictive across ages 12 to 26. Klaver, Lee and Rose put 219 undergraduates through the paradigm, got overall rates of 43% signing and 10% internalising, and found signing more likely among those with higher GSS Shift scores, under minimisation, and where the allegation was plausible. Horselenberg and colleagues found nothing in 2003 and, in 2006, only fantasy proneness, t(54) = 2.32, p = .02, with confessors at 7.8 against 5.8. Field data are split the same way. Kassin and Gudjonsson report that Sigurdsson and Gudjonsson compared 62 Icelandic inmates who said they had confessed falsely with other inmates, and found them more anxious, more compliant and more personality disordered, but no different in intelligence, verbal memory or suggestibility. The same authors returned to the question in 2001 with 509 inmates admitted over four years, of whom 62, or 12%, claimed a past false confession. Their abstract reports that of 17 psychological and 16 criminological and substance-abuse variables, the two that best separated the groups were the number of previous imprisonments and the score on the Gough Socialisation Scale.

study.cite: Horselenberg, R., Merckelbach, H., & Josephs, S. (2003). Individual differences and false confessions: A conceptual replication of Kassin and Kiechel (1996). Psychology, Crime & Law, 9(1), 1-8.

limits: This entry covers interrogative suggestibility and the questioning of witnesses and suspects. Implantation of whole childhood events is covered in the false memory entry, entry 35, which also carries the finding that being prone to one kind of memory error says little about being prone to another. Acceptance of misleading post-event information is entry 502, the misinformation effect, and taking a detail from another witness is entry 249, memory conformity. Kassin and colleagues draw the boundary the same way in 2025, reporting Ridley and Gudjonsson's distinction between immediate suggestibility, which the GSS measures at the moment of questioning, and delayed suggestibility, which is what misinformation experiments test. The search ran on 21 September 2026 across Crossref, PubMed, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, OpenAIRE, Semantic Scholar, the authors' own faculty pages and the open web. Several central documents were not read, and the reasons differ. Gudjonsson's 1984 paper, his 1986 model with Clark and the 1997 scale manual were not obtained. Unpaywall and OpenAIRE both record the 1984 paper as closed, and Elsevier's own page for it returned a Cloudflare bot block rather than a paywall notice. Redlich and Goodman's 2003 paper is closed at Springer, which serves an abstract and a subscription prompt, and no repository copy was found at Unpaywall, OpenAlex or Semantic Scholar, the last of which answered with an empty challenge page. Drizin and Leo's case series is open access at the University of North Carolina law repository, whose record page loads normally while the PDF itself is refused by a Cloudflare bot challenge. It is unread for that reason and not for a paywall, and its figures here are as Kassin and Gudjonsson report them. Sigurdsson and Gudjonsson's 1996 and 2001 papers are closed at Elsevier and at Taylor and Francis, both of which answered with bot challenges, and the Icelandic repository handle listed for the 2001 paper is dead. That paper's abstract was taken from OpenAlex and fetched twice. The key-placement and minimisation figures usually credited to Klaver come from a paper given at a conference in Edinburgh in July 2003, which has no DOI and was not located. They are quoted here as Kassin and Gudjonsson and as Horselenberg and colleagues report them. Stewart, Woody and Pulos's meta-analysis was read only in abstract at PubMed, so no pooled rate is given here; the abstract states the moderators and not the overall figure. Gignac and Powell published a psychometric critique of the scales in 2009 arguing about difference-score composites. It could not be obtained, Elsevier returned a bot block, and no source read here quotes its findings, so nothing is claimed about them. The scales are also bounded by what they measure. Yield 1 is close to an ordinary leading-question task, Shift is a response to negative feedback, and the two are not the same disposition. Nothing here bears on hypnotic suggestibility, on placebo response, or on the clinical dispute over recovered memories.
misreadings: The scale and the laboratory paradigms are treated as measures of one thing. They are not. Yield 1 counts acceptance of misleading questions and is close to what a misinformation experiment measures. Shift counts answers changed after an interviewer says the answers were wrong, which is a reaction to pressure and can move in either direction. Adding them into a Total is a convention, not a finding. The ALT-key study is quoted as showing that 69% of people will confess falsely. That figure is the share of the 75 analysed subjects, pooled across four conditions whose rates ran from 35% to 100%, and it is not an average of the four. Horselenberg's later work took the same paradigm to 11% by attaching a bill and to 8% by accusing students of exam fraud. Neither figure is the true rate; the rate is a property of the setup. The same study is also quoted in two incompatible ways by the same people. Kassin and Gudjonsson printed the four condition rates in 2004, and in 2025 the same authors described the result instead as a rise from 48% to 94% when a witness was added. Neither of those two numbers is in the 1996 paper, whose table gives 35 and 65 without a witness and 89 and 100 with one. High suggestibility is read as an explanation of who confesses. Otgaar and colleagues' pooled estimate is d = 0.33 in experiments and d = 1.09 in field samples, and the gap is the point, because the laboratory measures the trait in undergraduates with little at stake. Sigurdsson and Gudjonsson's inmates who claimed false confessions were not more suggestible than other inmates as a group. What distinguished them was compliance, which the Gudjonsson Compliance Scale measures and which is a different construct. Children's suggestibility is read as children being unreliable witnesses. Leichtman and Ceci's control preschoolers made no false allegations in free narrative at all, ten weeks on. The false reports appeared where adults had repeatedly suggested the events, and were worst where a prior stereotype had been planted as well. The other half of that study is the part usually dropped: 119 professionals who work on children's testimony watched the tapes and could not reliably separate the true reports from the false ones. Laboratory rates are also read as prevalence. They are not. The National Registry of Exonerations recorded 147 exonerations in the United States in 2024, of which 22, or 15%, involved a false confession. Gudjonsson's 2021 review reports self-reported false confession in about 20% of Icelandic prisoners and suspects, 33.4% of Scottish prisoners, and 13.8% of 2,726 European pupils of mean age 15.5 who had been questioned at a police station. Drizin and Leo's series of 125 proven false confessions in the United States between 1971 and 2002, as described by Kassin and Gudjonsson, was 93% male and 81% murder cases, with 63% of the confessors under 25 and 32% under 18, and 22% recorded as having mental retardation. A second 81% attaches to that series and means something else. It is the jury conviction rate, and it covers only the false confessors who pled not guilty and went to trial.

sources.text: Gudjonsson, G. H. (1984). A new scale of interrogative suggestibility. Personality and Individual Differences, 5(3), 303-314. The paper that introduced the GSS. Verified at Crossref; not read for this entry.

Kassin, S. M., & Gudjonsson, G. H. (2004). The psychology of confessions: A review of the literature and issues. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 5(2), 33-67. Read in full from the author's posted copy. Source for the description of the GSS, and for the Redlich and Goodman, Sigurdsson and Gudjonsson, Klaver and Drizin and Leo figures quoted at one remove. Its Table 5 of the Kassin and Kiechel condition means was checked against the 1996 paper and matches it exactly.

Kassin, S. M., Cleary, H. M. D., Gudjonsson, G. H., Leo, R. A., Meissner, C. A., Redlich, A. D., & Scherr, K. C. (2025). Police-induced confessions, 2.0: Risk factors and recommendations. Law and Human Behavior, 49(1), 7-53. The same authors' own update of the 2004 review, read in full. Source for the Gudjonsson and Clark definition with its page number, for the immediate-versus-delayed distinction, and for the 48% to 94% restatement of Kassin and Kiechel discussed under misreadings.

Kassin, S. M., & Kiechel, K. L. (1996). The social psychology of false confessions: Compliance, internalization, and confabulation. Psychological Science, 7(3), 125-128. The ALT-key study. Read in full from the scanned copy on Saul Kassin's own site, which an earlier version of this entry recorded as not obtainable. Source for the 79 recruited and 75 analysed, the pace settings, the cell percentages and the chi-square tests.

Horselenberg, R., Merckelbach, H., & Josephs, S. (2003). Individual differences and false confessions: A conceptual replication of Kassin and Kiechel (1996). Psychology, Crime & Law, 9(1), 1-8. Read in full. Note that the DOI printed on the paper itself, 10.1080/1068316021000057631, does not resolve at Crossref; the DOI given here does and matches the record.

Horselenberg, R., Merckelbach, H., Smeets, T., Franssens, D., Ygram Peters, G.-J., & Zeles, G. (2006). False confessions in the lab: Do plausibility and consequences matter? Psychology, Crime & Law, 12(1), 61-75. Read in full; source for the three studies at 77%, 11% and 8%, and for the Klaver, Gordon Rose and Lee conference figures quoted at one remove.

Otgaar, H., Schell-Leugers, J. M., Howe, M. L., De La Fuente Vilar, A., Houben, S. T. L., & Merckelbach, H. (2021). The link between suggestibility, compliance, and false confessions: A review using experimental and field studies. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 35(2), 445-455. Read in full from the KU Leuven repository copy; source for the pooled effect sizes across four experimental and five field studies.

Hein, F.-E., Scheuble, V., Beauducel, A., & Leue, A. (2021). Psychometric properties of a German online version of the Gudjonsson Suggestibility Scale 1. Frontiers in Psychology, 12, 718805. Source for the GSS 1 structure, the alphas, the means in a sample of 560 and the comparison with Gudjonsson's 1997 norms.

Frumkin, I. B., Lally, S. J., & Sexton, J. E. (2012). A United States forensic sample for the Gudjonsson Suggestibility Scales. Behavioral Sciences & the Law, 30(6), 749-763. Abstract read at PubMed; source for the 334-person forensic sample and the Yield-versus-Shift correlate pattern.
Leichtman, M. D., & Ceci, S. J. (1995). The effects of stereotypes and suggestions on preschoolers' reports. Developmental Psychology, 31(4), 568-578. Read in full; source for every Sam Stone figure.

Redlich, A. D., & Goodman, G. S. (2003). Taking responsibility for an act not committed: The influence of age and suggestibility. Law and Human Behavior, 27(2), 141-156. Abstract read at PubMed; the full paper was not obtained and its age-group percentages here are as Kassin and Gudjonsson (2004) report them.

Klaver, J., Lee, Z., & Rose, V. G. (2008). Effects of personality, interrogation techniques and plausibility in an experimental false confession paradigm. Legal and Criminological Psychology, 13(1), 71-88. Abstract read at Crossref; source for the 219 undergraduates, the 43% and 10% overall rates and the GSS Shift association. The ALT-versus-Esc and minimisation-versus-maximisation figures belong to a different report, a 2003 conference paper by Klaver, Gordon Rose and Lee, and are quoted here at one remove.

Sigurdsson, J. F., & Gudjonsson, G. H. (1996). The psychological characteristics of 'false confessors'. A study among Icelandic prison inmates and juvenile offenders. Personality and Individual Differences, 20(3), 321-329. Verified at Crossref; not obtained, and its findings here are as Kassin and Gudjonsson (2004) report them.

Sigurdsson, J. F., & Gudjonsson, G. H. (2001). False confessions: The relative importance of psychological, criminological and substance abuse variables. Psychology, Crime & Law, 7(4), 275-289. The same authors' larger follow-up. Abstract read at OpenAlex and fetched twice; the full paper was not obtained.

Stewart, J. M., Woody, W. D., & Pulos, S. (2018). The prevalence of false confessions in experimental laboratory simulations: A meta-analysis. Behavioral Sciences & the Law, 36(1), 12-31. Abstract read at PubMed; the moderator findings are quoted, the pooled rate was not obtained.

Gudjonsson, G. H. (2021). The science-based pathways to understanding false confessions and wrongful convictions. Frontiers in Psychology, 12, 633936. Source for the self-reported false confession rates in Iceland, Scotland and the seven-country school survey.

Gignac, G. E., & Powell, M. B. (2009). A psychometric evaluation of the Gudjonsson Suggestibility Scales: Problems associated with measuring suggestibility as a difference score composite. Personality and Individual Differences, 46(2), 88-93. Verified at Crossref; not obtained, and no claim is made here about what it found.

National Registry of Exonerations (2025, April 2). 2024 annual report. University of California Irvine Newkirk Center for Science and Society, University of Michigan Law School and Michigan State University College of Law. Page 4: 22 of the 147 exonerations recorded for 2024, or 15%, involved false confessions.
